title: You've never actually seen the Sun
script: You've never seen the Sun. Not the real one, anyway. The light hitting your eyes left it 8 minutes ago. If the Sun vanished right now, you'd still feel it shining for 8 whole minutes. You're always looking at the past.
description: Why every sunrise is an 8-minute-old replay.
music: Nebula - The Grey Room _ Density & Time.mp3

title: A teaspoon of this star weighs a billion tons
script: A teaspoon of this star weighs a billion tons. It's a neutron star, with more mass than our Sun crushed into a ball just 20 kilometers wide. It's so dense that protons and electrons merge into neutrons. That's where the name comes from.
description: The densest objects you can still call stars.

title: Saturn could float in your bathtub
script: Saturn could float in your bathtub. Well, almost. It's mostly hydrogen and helium, so it's less dense than water. The only problem? You'd need a bathtub more than 120,000 kilometers wide.
description: The planet that's lighter than water.
music: Turn In The Sun - Simon Herody.mp3

title: You can see 2.5 million years into the past
script: You can see 2.5 million years into the past. Tonight. Find the Andromeda galaxy on a dark night. That faint smudge is light that left before modern humans even existed. You're staring at ancient history.
description: The farthest thing you can see without a telescope.
music: Nebula - The Grey Room _ Density & Time.mp3

title: Your GPS only works because of Einstein
script: Your phone uses Einstein every single day. GPS satellite clocks run 38 microseconds a day faster than yours. Sounds tiny, right? But without fixing it, your map would be off by about 10 kilometers by tomorrow.
description: Relativity is in your pocket.

title: Mount Everest is tiny
script: Mount Everest is tiny. On Mars, Olympus Mons rises about 22 kilometers, two and a half times higher. It's so wide that from the top, its edges sink below the horizon. You'd barely know you're on a mountain.
description: Everest would look small on Mars.

title: 1.3 million Earths fit inside the Sun
script: 1.3 million Earths could fit inside the Sun. And the Sun? It's not even a big star. Some stars are around a thousand times wider. Next to them, our Sun is a tiny dot. Feeling small yet?
description: How small the Sun really is.
music: Nebula - The Grey Room _ Density & Time.mp3

title: You're 99.9999% empty space
script: You're 99.9999 percent empty space. Every atom in you is basically nothing. If an atom were a stadium, its nucleus would be a pea in the middle. So why don't you fall through your chair? Electrons push back.
description: The emptiness inside every atom.
music: Frame-Dragging - The Grey Room _ Density & Time.mp3

title: There's a dead star in your blood
script: There's a dead star in your blood. The iron in it was forged inside stars that burned out and exploded billions of years ago. Those atoms drifted through space and ended up in you. You're literally made of stardust.
description: Where the atoms in your body came from.

title: The Moon is slowly running away
script: The Moon is running away from us. Every year it drifts 3.8 centimeters farther, about as fast as your fingernails grow. We know because astronauts left mirrors up there, and scientists still bounce lasers off them.
description: The Moon is leaving us, very slowly.
music: Turn In The Sun - Simon Herody.mp3

title: The hottest planet isn't the closest one
script: The hottest planet isn't the closest one. Mercury hugs the Sun, but Venus is hotter. Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat like a blanket, pushing the surface to about 465 degrees Celsius. Hot enough to melt lead.
description: The greenhouse effect gone extreme.

title: Astronauts see 16 sunrises every day
script: Astronauts see 16 sunrises every day. The space station circles Earth every 90 minutes, at almost 28,000 kilometers per hour. That's fast enough to fly from London to New York in about 12 minutes.
description: Life at orbital speed.
music: Turn In The Sun - Simon Herody.mp3

title: This planet rolls around the Sun on its side
script: One planet rolls around the Sun on its side. Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees. So each pole gets around 42 years of nonstop sunlight, then 42 years of darkness. Scientists think a giant crash knocked it over.
description: The strangest seasons in the solar system.
music: Nebula - The Grey Room _ Density & Time.mp3

title: Moon footprints could last millions of years
script: Moon footprints can last millions of years. There's no wind or rain up there to erase them. Only tiny meteorites slowly wear them down. And orbiting cameras can still spot the astronauts' trails today.
description: Why the Apollo footprints are still there.
music: Frame-Dragging - The Grey Room _ Density & Time.mp3

title: Your head is older than your feet
script: Your head is older than your feet. Gravity slows down time, and it's a tiny bit weaker the higher you go. Scientists have actually measured the difference with atomic clocks, over a height of just 33 centimeters.
description: Einstein's time dilation, measured in a lab.
music: Frame-Dragging - The Grey Room _ Density & Time.mp3

title: Fold paper 42 times and it reaches the Moon
script: Paper can reach the Moon. Just fold it 42 times. Every fold doubles its thickness, so after 42 folds, a sheet a tenth of a millimeter thick becomes over 400,000 kilometers tall. You can't really fold it that much, but the math is real.
description: The terrifying power of doubling.
music: Turn In The Sun - Simon Herody.mp3

title: The Grand Canyon is tiny
script: The Grand Canyon is tiny. On Mars, a canyon called Valles Marineris stretches about 4,000 kilometers. That's almost ten times longer. It plunges up to 7 kilometers deep, five times deeper. Next to that Martian giant, ours is just a scratch.
description: The canyon on Mars that dwarfs the Grand Canyon.

title: The Moon is narrower than Australia
script: The Moon is narrower than Australia. The Moon is only about 3,475 kilometers across. Australia stretches almost 4,000 kilometers from coast to coast. It looks huge hanging in the night sky. But measure it side by side, and it's true.
description: Australia is wider than the Moon.

title: Sunsets on Mars are blue
script: Sunsets on Mars are blue. On Earth, air scatters blue light away, so sunsets glow red and orange. On Mars, fine dust lets blue light through more easily. NASA's Curiosity rover photographed it in 2015. On the red planet, the colors flip.
description: Why the Red Planet has blue sunsets.

title: A day on Venus is longer than its year
script: A day on Venus outlasts its year. Venus takes 243 Earth days to spin once. It circles the Sun in just 225 days. It even spins backwards, so the Sun rises in the west. So one Venus day outlasts its entire year.
description: The planet that spins slower than it orbits.

title: The Sun isn't actually yellow
script: The Sun isn't actually yellow. It shines in every color at once, making white light. Our air scatters some blue away, so near sunset it looks yellow or orange. From space, it's pure white. So forget every drawing you have ever seen.
description: The true color of the Sun.

title: Earth could shrink to the size of a marble
script: Earth could shrink to a marble. To become a black hole, our planet would need crushing into a ball about 2 centimeters wide. The Sun would need to fit in about 6 kilometers. Squeeze hard enough, and even a planet vanishes.
description: How small Earth would be as a black hole.

title: Jupiter has a storm bigger than Earth
script: Jupiter has a storm bigger than Earth. Called the Great Red Spot, it's wider than our whole planet. Its winds reach about 640 kilometers per hour. It has raged for at least 150 years. And it is still spinning right now.
description: The giant storm that could swallow our planet.

title: Saturn's rings are impossibly thin
script: Saturn's rings are impossibly thin. They stretch hundreds of thousands of kilometers from the planet. Yet the main rings are typically just 10 meters thick. Shrink them to a football field, and they'd be far thinner than paper.
description: The giant rings that are flatter than paper.

title: Astronauts grow taller in space
script: Astronauts grow taller in space. Without gravity pressing down, their spines relax and stretch out. Within just a few days, they can gain about 3 percent in height. Once they land, gravity squeezes them back down. But for a while, it's true.
description: What weightlessness does to your height.

title: Earth spins faster than the speed of sound
script: Earth spins faster than sound. At the equator, the ground carries you at over 1,600 kilometers per hour. Sound travels about 1,200. The ground, the air and everything around you move with you. You are flying right now and never notice.
description: The speed you never feel.

title: Every planet fits between Earth and the Moon
script: Every planet fits inside this gap. Stack Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Together they're about 388,000 kilometers wide. Usually, that's too much. But when the Moon is farthest, the gap is 397,000. Room to spare, which is why
description: Drawn to real scale: all seven planets, stacked in the space between us and the Moon.

title: Jupiter could swallow 1,300 Earths
script: Jupiter could swallow 1,300 Earths. That tiny dot is our whole planet. Fill Jupiter with Earths, and you'd need about 1,300. Line them across its middle, and 11 fit. Earth wouldn't even be a snack, because
description: Drawn to real scale: how many Earths it takes to fill the biggest planet.

title: How many Earths fit inside Saturn?
script: Saturn has room for 764 Earths. That little dot below it is Earth. Pour Earths into Saturn, and it takes 764 to fill it. Line them across its middle, and only 9 fit. Forget the famous rings, because even without them,
description: Drawn to real scale: how many Earths it takes to fill Saturn.

title: Jupiter is tiny next to the Sun
script: Jupiter is tiny next to the Sun. That dot is Jupiter, the biggest planet we have. Fill the Sun with Jupiters, and you'd need about 986. Line them across, and only 9 fit. And Jupiter alone holds 1,300 Earths, so
description: Drawn to real scale: how many Jupiters it takes to fill the Sun.

title: Exactly 4 Earths fit across Uranus
script: Exactly four Earths fit across Uranus. That small dot is our whole planet. Fill Uranus with Earths, and 63 fit inside. But line them across its middle, and it's four, with under 100 kilometers spare. It's such a tight fit that
description: Drawn to real scale: four Earths across Uranus, with less than 100 km to spare.

title: The Moon is smaller than you think
script: The Moon is smaller than you think. That little ball below Earth is the Moon. Fill Earth with Moons, and 49 fit inside. Line them across, and only 3 make it. It looks huge in the night sky, but
description: Drawn to real scale: how many Moons it takes to fill Earth.

title: What if the Sun became a black hole?
script: Crush the Sun into a black hole. It's 1,391,400 kilometers wide. Squeeze it into a ball just 5.9 kilometers across. Now not even light can escape. It's smaller than Mount Everest is tall. Only in a simulation can you
description: Drawn to real scale: the Sun squeezed down to its event horizon, about 6 km across.

title: Neptune's orbit fits inside this black hole
script: Neptune's orbit fits inside this black hole. Our galaxy's black hole is 24 million kilometers wide. It would fit inside Mercury's orbit. Now zoom out past every planet. M87's giant is 38 billion kilometers across. Every planet's orbit vanishes inside, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Sagittarius A* and M87* next to the planets' orbits. Masses from the Event Horizon Telescope.

title: Earth could fit in your hand
script: Earth could fit in your hand. It's 12,756 kilometers wide. Now crush all of it into a ball. At 1.8 centimeters, not even light escapes. That black hole is smaller than a coin. Every gram of Earth is still there, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Earth squeezed down to its event horizon, about 1.8 cm across.

title: The Sun is 109 Earths wide
script: The Sun is 109 Earths wide. See that tiny dot under it? That's Earth, with everyone you know. Now look back at the Sun. Line Earths up across its middle. Count every single one, and
description: Drawn to real scale: Earths lined up across the Sun's diameter.

title: The Moon is 30 Earths away
script: The Moon is 30 Earths away. Stack thirty of them in the gap. That's about 383,000 kilometers of planet. At the Moon's average distance, they don't fit. But when the Moon is farthest, they do. With nearly 15,000 kilometers to spare, because
description: Drawn to real scale: 30 Earths stacked in the gap between us and the Moon. Distances: NASA Moon fact sheet.

title: Neptune can shrink to 30 centimeters
script: Neptune can shrink to 30 centimeters. It's 49,528 kilometers wide. Squeeze every bit of it into a ball. Now not even light can escape. That's the length of a school ruler. Yet it still weighs as much as Neptune, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Neptune squeezed down to its event horizon, about 30 cm across. Mass: NASA Neptune fact sheet.

title: We're closest to the Sun in January
script: We're closest to the Sun in January. Stack 107 Suns in the gap. That's 149 million kilometers of Sun. In January, the gap is too short. By July, Earth drifts out, and they fit. So distance isn't why winter is cold, and
description: Drawn to real scale: 107 Suns stacked between Earth and the Sun. Distances: NASA Earth fact sheet.

title: Forty Suns fit between Mercury and the Sun
script: Forty Suns fit inside Mercury's gap. Line them up toward Mercury. They span about 56 million kilometers. When Mercury swings close, they slam into it. When it swings out, they fit. With 13 million kilometers to spare, because
description: Drawn to real scale: forty Suns lined up between the Sun and Mercury. Distances: NASA Mercury fact sheet.

title: Mars is only half Earth's size
script: Mars is only half Earth's size. That red ball below Earth is Mars. It's 6,792 kilometers wide, about half of us. Yet its surface roughly matches all of Earth's dry land. Every desert and city of ours could fit there, because
description: Drawn to real scale: Mars next to Earth. Surface area: ESA Mars facts.

title: Mercury is barely bigger than our Moon
script: Mercury is barely bigger than our Moon. That smaller ball below it is the Moon. Mercury is 4,879 kilometers wide, and the Moon is 3,475. Two moons, Ganymede and Titan, are even wider than Mercury. It's a real planet, and yet
description: Drawn to real scale: the Moon next to Mercury. Sizes: NASA fact sheets.

title: Neptune is smaller than Uranus, yet heavier
script: Neptune is smaller than Uranus, yet heavier. That blue world below Uranus is Neptune. It's 1,590 kilometers narrower. But it packs about 18 percent more mass into less space. The smaller twin is the heavyweight, which means
description: Drawn to real scale: Neptune next to Uranus. Masses: NASA planetary fact sheet.

title: The Moon can hide the whole Sun
script: The Moon can hide the whole Sun. That speck below it is our Moon. The Sun is 400 times wider. It's also about 400 times farther away. Fill the Sun with Moons, you'd need 64 million. That lucky match is why
description: Drawn to real scale: the Moon next to the Sun, the size match behind total eclipses.

title: Venus is almost exactly Earth's size
script: Venus is almost exactly Earth's size. That ball below Earth is Venus. It's 12,104 kilometers wide, 95 percent of us. Same size, but its surface is hot enough to melt lead. Our twin turned into a furnace, even though
description: Drawn to real scale: Venus next to Earth. Sizes: NASA fact sheets.

title: The Moon could become a grain of sand
script: The Moon could become a sand grain. It's 3,475 kilometers wide. Crush every bit of it into a ball. At 0.2 millimeters, not even light escapes. That's smaller than a grain of sand. And it would still pull our tides, so
description: Drawn to real scale: the Moon squeezed down to its event horizon, about 0.2 mm across. Mass: NASA Moon fact sheet.

title: Venus could hide behind a dime
script: Venus could hide behind a dime. It's 12,104 kilometers wide. Squeeze all of it down into a ball. At 1.4 centimeters, light can't escape. A dime covers it completely. And it would weigh just as much as before, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Venus squeezed down to its event horizon, about 1.4 cm across. Mass: NASA Venus fact sheet.

title: Saturn could shrink to your height
script: Saturn could shrink to your height. It's 120,536 kilometers wide, without the rings. Crush the whole planet into a ball. At 1.7 meters, not even light gets out. That's about as tall as you are. And its moons would keep orbiting, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Saturn squeezed down to its event horizon, about 1.7 m across. Mass: NASA Saturn fact sheet.

title: Jupiter doesn't really orbit the Sun
script: Jupiter doesn't really orbit the Sun. That dot below the Sun is Jupiter, our biggest planet. It's so heavy it tugs the Sun around. They both circle a point just outside the Sun's surface. So the Sun wobbles too, and
description: Drawn to real scale: Jupiter next to the Sun. Barycenter: NASA Space Place.

title: Mercury has ice
script: Mercury has ice. That speck below the Sun is Mercury, the closest planet. Its days hit 430 degrees Celsius. But deep craters at its poles never see the Sun. Water ice hides inside them, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Mercury next to the Sun. Temperatures and polar ice: NASA Mercury facts.

title: Uranus would fit on your plate
script: Uranus would fit on your plate. It's 51,118 kilometers wide. Now press the whole planet together. At about 26 centimeters across, even light is trapped. That's about a dinner plate. It would still hold its 28 moons, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Uranus squeezed down to its event horizon, about 26 cm across. Mass: NASA Uranus fact sheet.

title: The fastest winds blow on Neptune
script: The fastest winds blow on Neptune. That small ball below it is Earth. Even our worst hurricanes would look gentle there. Neptune's winds hit 2,000 kilometers an hour, faster than sound. And it's the farthest planet from the Sun, yet
description: Drawn to real scale: Earth next to Neptune. Wind speed: NASA/Caltech Cool Cosmos.

title: The Moon has no dark side
script: The Moon has no dark side. That gray ball below Earth is the Moon. It turns once every 27 days, one full orbit. So we only ever see one face. But the far side gets just as much sunlight, so
description: Drawn to real scale: the Moon next to Earth. Rotation: NASA Moon fact sheet; far side: NASA StarChild.

title: Venus has the roundest orbit of any planet
script: Venus has the roundest orbit. Stack 77 Suns between it and the Sun. They stretch 107 million kilometers. At its closest, Venus is too near. At its farthest, it's barely one Sun farther. That leaves 1.1 million kilometers to spare, because
description: Drawn to real scale: 77 Suns stacked between Venus and the Sun. Distances: NASA Venus fact sheet.

title: Jupiter's day lasts under 10 hours
script: Jupiter's day lasts under 10 hours. That tiny dot below it is Earth. Earth needs 24 hours to spin. Jupiter spins once every 9.9 hours. It's 11 Earths wide, and its equator moves over 45,000 kilometers an hour. Sunsets come fast, because
description: Drawn to real scale: Earth next to Jupiter, the planet with the shortest day. Rotation: NASA Jupiter fact sheet.

title: Saturn has nearly 300 moons
script: Saturn has nearly 300 moons. That speck below it is our Moon, for scale. Earth gets just this one. Most of Saturn's moons are only a few kilometers wide. Astronomers keep finding more, so
description: Drawn to real scale: our Moon next to Saturn. Moon count: IAU Minor Planet Center (293 as of mid-2026).

title: All of Mars could fit in a mustard seed
script: All of Mars in a mustard seed. Mars is 6,792 kilometers wide. Crush the red planet down. At 1.9 millimeters, it's a black hole. A mustard seed is barely bigger. Its two moons would keep circling, and that's
description: Drawn to real scale: Mars squeezed down to its event horizon, about 1.9 mm across. Mass: NASA Mars fact sheet.

title: Uranus is the coldest planet, not Neptune
script: Uranus is the coldest planet. That little world beneath it is Earth. Earth averages a mild 15 degrees Celsius. Uranus has hit minus 224, colder than distant Neptune. Scientists think an ancient crash let its heat escape, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Earth next to Uranus. Temperatures: NASA planetary fact sheet and Uranus facts.

title: The Sun is basically our whole solar system
script: The Sun is our solar system. That ringed dot below it is Saturn, the second biggest planet. Add up every planet, moon and asteroid. Together they're less than 0.2 percent of the mass. The other 99.8 percent is the Sun, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Saturn next to the Sun. Mass share: NASA Sun facts.

title: Mercury could pass for a poppy seed
script: Mercury could pass for a poppy seed. It's 4,879 kilometers wide. Pack all that rock into one ball. At one millimeter, it turns into a black hole. That's a poppy seed. It would still orbit the Sun every 88 days, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Mercury squeezed down to its event horizon, about 1 mm across. Mass: NASA Mercury fact sheet.

title: Venus's air would crush you
script: Venus's air would crush you. That ball below Earth is Venus, almost our twin. But its air presses down 92 times harder than ours. That's like being 900 meters under the ocean. Even the toughest lander survived about two hours, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Venus next to Earth. Pressure: NASA Venus fact sheet; lander record: Venera 13, 127 minutes.

title: Jupiter can barely get any bigger
script: Jupiter can barely get any bigger. That ringed world below it is Saturn. It's 84 percent as wide, with under a third the mass. Pile on more mass, and Jupiter hardly grows. Add even more, and gravity squeezes it smaller, so
description: Drawn to real scale: Saturn next to Jupiter. Masses: NASA planetary fact sheet; mass-radius: Seager et al. 2007.
